title: Computer punched cards were the size of a 19th-century dollar bill

cover.alt: A used punched card with columns of small rectangular holes and a line of printed characters along its top edge.

body: Herman Hollerith developed punched-card data processing for the **1890 US census**, after the 1880 count had taken eight years to process. His early cards had round holes in 12 rows and 24 columns, and the standard card size adopted soon after, 3¼ by 7⅜ inches (83 × 187 mm), was exactly the size of the US paper currency printed from 1862 to 1923. IBM's famous 80-column card of 1928 kept those dimensions, and they stayed the shape of data entry until the mid-1980s. By 1937 IBM's plant in Endicott, New York, was printing 5 to 10 million cards every day.

slides.alt: A warehouse aisle lined with tall stacks of boxes of punched cards on pallets.
slides.caption: Punched cards stored at the US Federal Records Center in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1959: pallets of boxes holding 2,000 cards each.

slides.question: How many years did it take to process the 1880 US census by hand?
slides.explanation: Eight years. For 1890, clerks punched about 100 million cards and Herman Hollerith's [tabulating machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabulating_machine) finished the count months early.

slides.label: characters on one IBM card, one per column
slides.text: The 1928 card had 80 columns and 10 rows; two rows were added in 1930 so letters could be coded as combinations of holes.

slides.heading: How Hollerith's 1890 tabulator read a card

steps.label: A clerk punches holes for age, sex and state
The card rests over small cups of mercury
Spring-loaded wires drop through the holes
A circuit closes and a counter dial advances

events.text: Hollerith's cards count the US census
He founds the Tabulating Machine Company
Its successor company is renamed IBM

slides.question: How did Hollerith's 1890 machine sense a hole in a card?
options: A wire dipped into mercury below
A beam of light shone through it
A magnet read the punched edge
Air blew through and moved a lever
slides.explanation: Spring-loaded wires pressed on the card; where there was a hole, a wire dipped into a cup of mercury below, completing a circuit that advanced a counter.
